title: Cynics and Sceptics
orientation: This chapter covers two of the four Hellenistic schools founded after Alexander: Cynicism (Antisthenes and Diogenes), a doctrine of radical self-sufficiency achieved by rejecting convention and desire, and Scepticism (Pyrrho, Timon, and the sceptical Academy of Arcesilaus, Carneades, and Clitomachus), a doctrine that denies the possibility of certain knowledge. Both are presented by Russell as responses to the same historical condition described in Chapter XXV: the individual's loss of power over the political world, which pushes philosophy toward private, defensive strategies for inner peace.
historical_background: Russell frames the chapter with a general reflection on how intellectuals relate to their societies -- sometimes comfortably, sometimes as revolutionaries, sometimes in despair -- and argues that Greek philosophy after Aristotle moves decisively toward the despairing, other-worldly end of this spectrum because political power had passed entirely into Macedonian hands. He also narrates two set-piece Roman episodes: Carneades's scandalous 156 B.C. embassy lectures at Rome, and the clash between Carneades's scepticism and the elder Cato's austere traditionalism, as evidence of how Greek philosophy was received (and resisted) at Rome.
philosophical_problems: If political virtue can no longer be exercised in a good state, what does virtue consist in for the private individual?
Can the senses or reason ever give certain knowledge, or must every claim to knowledge be doubted?
Is thoroughgoing philosophical doubt itself a dogmatic position, and if so, is it self-undermining?
If certainty is unattainable, can degrees of probability still guide rational action?
Is a life of studied indifference to worldly goods (Cynicism) actually virtuous, or does its popularized form collapse into self-serving irresponsibility?

philosophers_discussed.name: Antisthenes
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: A disciple of Socrates who, after Socrates's death, rejected refined philosophy and worldly conventions (government, private property, marriage, established religion) in favor of a 'return to nature' and simple goodness accessible to the plain man; founder of the outlook that becomes Cynicism through his pupil Diogenes.

philosophers_discussed.name: Diogenes of Sinope
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Antisthenes's pupil and the school's namesake ('cynic' = 'canine'); lived by begging, rejected all convention of dress, housing, and decency, and sought virtue and freedom through liberation from desire and indifference to fortune's gifts -- famously asking Alexander only to 'stand out of my light.'

philosophers_discussed.name: Teles
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: A popularizing Cynic preacher of the early third century B.C. whose surviving sermons show how Cynic doctrine, diluted for a general audience in Alexandria, degenerated into a self-serving indifference toward one's obligations to others (e.g., minimizing gratitude owed to a benefactor).

philosophers_discussed.name: Pyrrho
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Founder of formal Scepticism as a school doctrine; accompanied Alexander's army to India, then retired to Elis; systematized older doubts about sense-perception into a general scepticism about ethics and logic as well, holding there could never be rational grounds for preferring one course of action over another.

philosophers_discussed.name: Timon
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Pyrrho's disciple, who advanced the strongest intellectual argument for Scepticism: since all Greek deductive logic must start from unprovable first principles, and Timon denies any such principles are self-evident, all argument is either circular or an infinite regress, so nothing can be proved. He anticipates Hume in distinguishing valid inference about repeatedly observed conjunctions from invalid inference about unobserved entities like atoms.

philosophers_discussed.name: Arcesilaus
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Head of Plato's Academy who redirected it toward Scepticism by treating Platonic dialectic (the inconclusive, aporetic side of Plato's dialogues) as an end in itself; taught by refuting any thesis a pupil proposed and by arguing opposite sides of a question on different days, leaving the Academy sceptical for roughly two centuries.

philosophers_discussed.name: Carneades
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Head of the sceptical Academy who, on a diplomatic mission to Rome in 156 B.C., scandalously gave one lecture praising Plato and Aristotle's view of justice and a second lecture demolishing it, arguing that great states are built on successful injustice; provoked the elder Cato's hostility to Greek philosophy. Also developed, with Clitomachus, a constructive doctrine of degrees of probability as a practical guide to action.

philosophers_discussed.name: Cato the Elder
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Roman statesman embodying the 'stern, stiff, stupid, and brutal' traditional Roman moral code; personally austere and honest but casually cruel to his slaves; opposed Carneades's lectures and Greek philosophical education generally, fearing it would corrupt Roman youth away from martial virtue.

philosophers_discussed.name: Clitomachus (born Hasdrubal)
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: A Carthaginian who succeeded Carneades as head of the Academy; prolific writer (reportedly over 400 books) who continued Carneades's doctrine of probability and, with him, campaigned against belief in divination, magic, and astrology.

philosophers_discussed.name: Aenesidemus
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Revived pure Scepticism after Clitomachus, rejecting the Academy's doctrine of probability and reverting to the earliest, most thoroughgoing form of Pyrrhonism.

philosophers_discussed.name: Sextus Empiricus
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The only ancient Sceptic philosopher whose works survive; Russell quotes his treatise 'Arguments Against Belief in a God,' which shows Sceptics conforming outwardly to conventional religious practice while suspending belief, and which argues that affirming God's existence forces an impious choice between making God the author of evil or admitting He is grudging or impotent.

schools_discussed: The sceptical phase of Plato's Academy

core_concepts.name: Cynic self-sufficiency through rejection of convention
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The Cynics held that true virtue and freedom come from wanting as little as possible from the world, so that nothing external -- poverty, insult, loss -- can touch you. Diogenes lived this out literally, owning almost nothing and living by begging.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine that virtue and moral freedom consist in liberation from desire for external, fortune-dependent goods (wealth, honour, comfort, convention), achieved by deliberately rejecting the artificial trappings of civilization ('defacing the coinage' of all conventional values).
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell treats it as the doctrine's most valuable core, later inherited wholesale by the Stoics, though the Stoics -- unlike the Cynics -- did not reject the amenities of civilization itself.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Develops from Antisthenes (a disciple of Socrates) through his pupil Diogenes of Sinope in the fourth century B.C., though its temper, Russell notes, belongs to the Hellenistic age despite predating it slightly.
examples: Diogenes living by begging and owning almost nothing
His reply to Alexander's offer of any favor: 'only to stand out of my light'
Diogenes's view that Prometheus was justly punished for giving mankind the arts of civilization
objections: Popularized Cynicism (Teles) degenerated into using 'indifference to goods' as an excuse to accept charity without gratitude or obligation
competing_positions: Stoicism, which retained the ideal of indifference to fortune but did not reject civilized life itself
The Taoists, Rousseau, and Tolstoy, whom Russell compares to Diogenes but judges less consistent
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly absorbed into Stoic ethics (Ch. XXVIII): indifference to external fortune as the basis of virtue and freedom.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Rejects government, private property, marriage, and established religion outright.

core_concepts.name: Pyrrhonist Scepticism as 'dogmatic doubt'
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Pyrrho and his followers did not just say 'I'm not sure' about this or that; they claimed to know, for certain, that nobody can ever know anything. Russell points out this is itself a strong (and self-undermining) claim to knowledge, unlike ordinary scientific caution or curiosity.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The Sceptic position, distinguished by Russell from both scientific caution ('I think it is so, but am not sure') and open inquiry ('I don't know, but hope to find out'), which asserts as a settled conclusion that 'nobody knows, and nobody ever can know' -- a dogmatic claim about the impossibility of knowledge.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Identifies, for Russell, the central logical weakness of ancient Scepticism: its claim to certainty about universal uncertainty.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Systematized by Pyrrho (who served in Alexander's army and traveled to India) after earlier Greek doubts about sense-perception (going back to the Sophists, notably Protagoras and Gorgias).
examples: Pyrrho's alleged view that there can never be rational grounds for preferring one course of action to another
The practical upshot: a Sceptic conforms outwardly to local custom (attending temple rituals, even serving as a priest) while inwardly withholding belief
objections: Sceptics deny they dogmatically assert the impossibility of knowledge, but Russell finds their denials 'not very convincing'
competing_positions: Parmenides's and Plato's opposite dogmatism, which denies the cognitive value of perception in order to assert certain, purely intellectual knowledge
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Timon's arguments 'cut at the root' of the Aristotelian philosophy that later dominated the Middle Ages, since they attack the very possibility of self-evident first premises for deduction.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Practically compatible with conventional religious observance, since Sceptics conform to custom without asserting belief.

core_concepts.name: Timon's regress argument against certain knowledge
core_concepts.plain_explanation: All Greek logical proof works by deducing conclusions from general starting principles. But if you can never be sure those starting principles are true, then any 'proof' either goes in a circle or hangs from nothing -- so nothing is really proved.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Timon's argument that, since Greek deductive logic requires self-evident general first premises, and no such premises can be shown to be self-evident, all deductive argument is either circular or an infinite, unsupported chain, and hence no genuine proof of anything is possible.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell singles this out as intellectually 'very hard to answer' from within the framework of Greek logic, and notes it strikes directly at the foundations of the Aristotelian system that dominated medieval philosophy.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Advanced by Timon, Pyrrho's disciple, in the third century B.C.
examples: Two surviving fragments distinguishing what 'appears' (valid) from what one asserts as objectively true, e.g. 'That honey is sweet I refuse to assert; that it appears sweet, I fully grant.'
objections: A modern Sceptic, Russell notes, would go further and say that even 'honey appears sweet' is only highly probable, since any statement about a phenomenon is distinct from the phenomenon itself and so can, in principle, be false
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell compares Timon's doctrine -- valid inference from repeated observed conjunction, invalid inference to unobserved entities like atoms -- to the epistemology of David Hume.

core_concepts.name: Academic probabilism (Carneades and Clitomachus)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Even if you can never be absolutely certain of anything, some beliefs are still much more likely to be true than others, and it is reasonable to act on whichever hypothesis is most probable.
core_concepts.precise_definition: A constructive doctrine developed within the sceptical Academy holding that, although certainty is unattainable, degrees of probability can and should guide practical action and belief.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell notes this is a view 'with which most modern philosophers would agree,' making it the most philosophically durable contribution of the sceptical Academy, though the original texts explaining it are lost.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed by Carneades and continued by his successor Clitomachus in the second century B.C.
examples: Carneades's and Clitomachus's shared campaign against belief in divination, magic, and astrology, treated as unjustified by any real evidence of probability
objections: Later revived pure Scepticism (Aenesidemus) explicitly rejected the probability doctrine as an unwarranted concession to dogmatism
competing_positions: Aenesidemus's reversion to unmitigated Pyrrhonist doubt
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Used to argue against popular Hellenistic superstition (divination, astrology).

core_concepts.name: Scepticism's tolerant, hostile-to-religion character and Sextus Empiricus's case against theism
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Later Sceptics went along with ordinary religious rituals as a matter of custom while refusing to actually believe the underlying doctrines, and some, like Sextus Empiricus, wrote direct arguments that believing in a providential god leads either to blaming God for evil or admitting God is weak or uncaring.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The distinction, illustrated by Sextus Empiricus's surviving treatise, between practical conformity to religious custom and intellectual assent to religious belief, together with an early version of the problem of evil used as an argument against dogmatic theism.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Shows Scepticism functioning as a mainly negative, corrosive force against dogmatic religion in antiquity, without the positive scientific alternative that later, modern scepticism would pair with.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Late ancient Scepticism, transmitted through Sextus Empiricus (second-third century A.D.), possibly drawing on Carneades via Clitomachus.
examples: 'If they say that God controls everything, they make Him the author of evil things; if... He controls some things only, or nothing, they are compelled to make God either grudging or impotent'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly targets dogmatic theism, while endorsing outward conformity to state religious practice.

arguments.title: Timon's regress argument against the possibility of proof
premises: All Greek deductive logic (modeled on Euclid) proceeds from general first principles taken as self-evident.
No general first principle can actually be shown to be self-evident (there is no method for proving a first premise, since proving it would require a further premise).
Therefore any chain of argument either loops back on itself (circular) or extends backward forever without ever reaching a genuinely self-evident starting point.
arguments.conclusion: Nothing can be proved by argument.
arguments.explanation: Russell notes this argument is 'very hard to answer' from within Greek logic's own assumptions, because it does not deny particular observations but attacks the structural requirement of all deduction: a secure starting point. It anticipates, and in Russell's view foreshadows, the later collapse of confidence in Aristotelian first principles.
objections: The Stoics later claimed certain principles are 'luminously obvious' and universally admitted (consensus gentium), effectively asserting the self-evidence Timon denied is possible
implications: Undermines the entire deductive edifice of Aristotelian philosophy, which Russell notes dominated medieval thought.
Motivates the later Academic move toward probabilism rather than certainty as the standard for rational belief.

arguments.title: Carneades's argument that justice is not always advantageous to its practitioner
premises: Great states, including Rome, have become great through successful unjust aggression against weaker neighbours.

In situations of extreme personal danger (a shipwreck, or fleeing a victorious enemy), a person who seizes another's means of survival (a plank, a wounded comrade's horse) improves his own chances at another's expense.
In such cases the unjust actor benefits and the just actor (who refrains) is disadvantaged or dies.
arguments.conclusion: The Platonic/Socratic claim that inflicting injustice always harms the perpetrator more than the victim does not hold up under examination; injustice can straightforwardly benefit its perpetrator.
arguments.explanation: This is the second of Carneades's paired 156 B.C. Rome lectures, deliberately built to overturn the first day's edifying defense of Platonic/Aristotelian justice. Russell presents it as a piece of sceptical method (arguing both sides with equal skill) rather than as a sincere ethical position of Carneades's own.
objections: Cato the Elder's reaction -- alarm that such reasoning would corrupt Roman youth -- functions as an implicit practical objection: even if logically forceful, the argument is socially corrosive
implications: Illustrates the sceptical Academy's method of arguing both sides of a question with equal plausibility, which Russell says taught pupils only 'cleverness and indifference to truth.'

key_distinctions: Genuine Cynic asceticism (Diogenes) vs. popularized Cynic sermonizing (Teles) that excuses self-interest
Scientific/inquiring doubt ('I don't know, but hope to find out') vs. dogmatic Scepticism ('nobody knows, and nobody ever can know')
Belief about phenomena/appearances (e.g. 'honey appears sweet') vs. belief about objective fact (e.g. 'honey is sweet')
Certainty vs. degrees of probability as a guide to action (the Academic contribution of Carneades and Clitomachus)
Outward conformity to religious custom vs. inward assent to religious doctrine, as practiced by ancient Sceptics
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Antisthenes is placed as a direct disciple of Socrates, carrying forward Socratic simplicity and indifference to comfort into a far more radical rejection of civilization. Scepticism about the senses is traced back to the Sophists (Protagoras, Gorgias) and to the opposite dogmatism of Parmenides and Plato, who denied perception's cognitive value in favor of pure intellect. Arcesilaus's redirection of the Academy toward Scepticism works by reinterpreting the inconclusive, aporetic strand already present in Plato's own dialogues (e.g. the Parmenides).
connections_to_later_philosophers: Cynic indifference to external fortune passes directly into Stoicism (Ch. XXVIII), though the Stoics keep the amenities of civilization the Cynics rejected. Timon's scepticism about unobserved entities (like atoms) and his acceptance of inference from repeated conjunction is compared explicitly by Russell to David Hume. Timon's regress argument against self-evident first principles is said to strike at the Aristotelian philosophy that dominated the Middle Ages.
political_social_context: The chapter's central Roman episode is political: Carneades's 156 B.C. diplomatic mission to Rome and his scandalous lectures, set against Cato the Elder's fear that Greek philosophical education would corrupt Roman martial and civic virtue -- an early and vivid case of Greek philosophy colliding with Roman traditionalism.
religion_science_culture_context: Both schools bear on religion: Cynicism rejects established religion outright as an artificial convention; Scepticism, by contrast, permits (and its adherents practiced) full outward participation in pagan religious ritual, including serving as priests, while suspending inward belief -- illustrated by Sextus Empiricus's argument against dogmatic theism.
russell_presentation: Russell treats Cynicism and Scepticism as two Hellenistic strategies for coping with the same underlying condition described in Chapter XXV: the individual's loss of power over public affairs. He is sympathetic to Diogenes's personal sincerity and vigour but views the doctrine, once popularized (Teles), as degenerating into a self-serving excuse for accepting others' generosity without gratitude. On Scepticism, Russell's central analytical move is to distinguish it sharply from scientific open-mindedness, calling it 'dogmatic doubt' -- itself a confident claim that knowledge is impossible -- and he credits Timon's regress argument as a genuinely strong challenge to Greek deductive logic. He gives real weight to the Carneades-Clitomachus doctrine of probability as anticipating a view modern philosophers largely accept, while treating the vivid Carneades-versus-Cato episode as illustrating both the seductive cleverness and the moral hollowness that sceptical rhetoric could produce when detached from sincere conviction. He closes by noting that Scepticism, though intellectually formidable, offered nothing positive to replace the popular religion it discredited, leaving 'the way... left clear for an invasion of oriental religions' -- his direct bridge into the Epicurean and Stoic material and, eventually, Christianity.
critical_context: Interpretive note: Russell's characterization of ancient Scepticism as lacking any 'supplement' comparable to modern science is a comparative judgment made from his own twentieth-century, science-oriented vantage point; some historians of ancient philosophy would stress that Academic probabilism (Carneades/Clitomachus) functioned, within its own terms, as exactly this kind of alternative -- a rational, non-dogmatic basis for everyday judgment and action -- rather than treating its loss as simply a gap Scepticism failed to fill.
key_takeaways: Cynicism (Antisthenes, Diogenes) sought virtue and freedom through radical indifference to external goods and rejection of civilized convention; its popularized version (Teles) degenerated into self-serving excuse-making.

Pyrrhonist Scepticism held that no rational grounds exist for preferring any belief or action over another, but Russell calls this 'dogmatic doubt' because it confidently asserts the impossibility of knowledge.

Timon's regress argument -- that Greek deductive logic cannot supply self-evident first principles, so nothing can be proved -- is presented as intellectually formidable and later relevant to the collapse of Aristotelian authority.
Arcesilaus turned Plato's own Academy sceptical for roughly two centuries by treating the inconclusive side of Plato's dialogues as the whole of his philosophy.
Carneades's paired 156 B.C. Rome lectures (defending, then demolishing, Platonic justice) scandalized Cato the Elder and illustrate Scepticism's rhetorical double-edged sword.
Carneades and Clitomachus developed a doctrine of probability as a practical guide to action despite unattainable certainty -- a view Russell says most modern philosophers would endorse.
Ancient Scepticism, lacking any positive alternative comparable to modern science, ultimately left room for the spread of 'oriental' religions and, eventually, Christianity.
study_notes:
Keep the two schools in this chapter conceptually separate even though Russell links them by common historical cause. Cynicism is an ethical strategy: reduce your desires until fortune has nothing left to threaten. Scepticism is an epistemological strategy: withhold belief until certainty is impossible to demand, and therefore impossible to be disappointed by. Both, in Russell's reading, are defensive: they aim not at achieving some positive good but at making the individual invulnerable to a world he cannot control -- exactly the problem set up in Chapter XXV.

Pay special attention to Russell's distinction between ordinary scientific doubt and Pyrrhonist 'dogmatic doubt.' This distinction matters well beyond antiquity: it is the same charge often leveled at any radical scepticism (ancient or modern) -- that claiming certainty about the impossibility of certainty is self-refuting or at least self-undermining. Also notice how the chapter foreshadows a recurring pattern in the rest of Part III: a philosophy begins with a sharp, austere original insight (Diogenes's genuine self-sufficiency, Pyrrho's genuine doubt) and is then popularized into something looser and more self-serving (Teles's sermons, later lax scepticism) -- a pattern you will see again with Epicureanism and Stoicism.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A follower of Diogenes's philosophy of rejecting material comfort, social convention, and desire in order to be free from fortune's power over you; originally meant 'dog-like' because of Diogenes's deliberately shameless lifestyle.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A member of the philosophical tradition founded by Antisthenes and exemplified by Diogenes of Sinope, holding that virtue and freedom are achieved through the rejection of conventional social, material, and religious attachments ('defacing the coinage' of accepted values).

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The philosophical position that certain knowledge is impossible, so the wise response is to suspend judgment about how things really are, while still going along with ordinary customs in practice.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The school founded by Pyrrho, holding that no rational grounds exist for preferring one belief or course of action to another, extending traditional Greek doubts about sense-perception into a general doubt about ethics and logic, while distinguishing valid claims about how things 'appear' from unwarranted claims about how things objectively 'are.'

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Russell's term for Scepticism's real character: not humble uncertainty, but a confident assertion that knowledge is definitely impossible.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Russell's characterization of ancient Pyrrhonist Scepticism as itself a dogmatic position -- asserting with confidence the universal negative claim that 'nobody knows, and nobody ever can know' -- as distinct from either scientific probabilism or open inquiry.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea, developed within Plato's sceptical Academy, that even without certainty, some beliefs are more likely true than others and should guide action.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The constructive doctrine, associated with Carneades and Clitomachus, that degrees of probability, though never amounting to certainty, provide a rational and sufficient basis for belief and practical action.

questions.prompt: What did Diogenes mean when he said his father's project of 'defacing the coinage' should be pursued on a much larger scale?
questions.answer: Diogenes's father had literally been imprisoned for defacing coins; Diogenes reinterpreted this as a metaphor for rejecting all false conventional 'stamps' of value -- honour, wisdom, riches, and titles like general or king -- which he considered as false as debased coinage.
questions.explanation: This is Russell's quoted image (from Gilbert Murray) capturing the essence of Cynic philosophy as a rejection of all conventional valuations.

questions.prompt: Contrast Diogenes's original Cynicism with the popularized Cynic preaching of Teles that Russell describes.
questions.answer: Diogenes practiced genuine, radical self-denial and indifference to comfort as a path to virtue and freedom. Teles's popularized sermons, by contrast, taught a comfortable 'indifference' that let a borrower minimize gratitude to a lender or the wealthy console themselves that the poor's sufferings were merely imaginary -- Russell notes this stage makes it 'difficult to feel any sympathy with the simple life, which has grown altogether too simple.'
questions.explanation: This shows Russell tracking the degeneration of a serious philosophical doctrine into a self-serving popular fashion.

questions.prompt: How does Russell distinguish philosophical Scepticism from ordinary scientific caution or intellectual curiosity?
questions.answer: The scientist says 'I think it is so-and-so, but I am not sure'; the curious person says 'I don't know, but I hope to find out'; the philosophical Sceptic says 'nobody knows, and nobody ever can know' -- a dogmatic, closed claim rather than an open, provisional one.
questions.explanation: Russell calls this element of Scepticism 'dogmatic doubt,' and argues it is what makes the system logically vulnerable.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Timon's argument that nothing can ever be proved, and explain why Russell considers it especially significant for later philosophy.
questions.answer: Premise: Greek deductive logic requires starting from general first principles taken as self-evident. Premise: No method exists for proving such first principles (proving them would itself require some further premise). Conclusion: Every chain of argument is either circular or an infinite regress with no secure foundation, so nothing can genuinely be proved. Russell notes this argument strikes at the root of the Aristotelian philosophy that dominated the Middle Ages.
questions.explanation: Timon's regress argument is presented as one of the few genuinely strong intellectual arguments in ancient Scepticism.

questions.prompt: Which head of Plato's Academy turned it toward Scepticism for roughly two centuries, and by what method did he teach?
questions.answer: Arcesilaus; he maintained no thesis of his own, instead refuting whatever thesis a pupil proposed, and sometimes argued opposite conclusions with equal skill on successive occasions.
questions.explanation: Arcesilaus achieved this by treating the inconclusive, dialectical side of Plato's own dialogues as the whole of Plato's philosophy.

questions.prompt: Describe the incident involving Carneades at Rome in 156 B.C. and its consequence.
questions.answer: Sent to Rome on a diplomatic mission, Carneades gave a first lecture praising Plato and Aristotle's view of justice, then a second lecture systematically demolishing it (arguing, e.g., that great states are built on successful injustice, and that self-preservation can justify taking a weaker or wounded person's means of survival). This scandalized the elder Cato, who moved to have the philosophers sent home, fearing Greek learning would corrupt Roman youth.
questions.explanation: Russell uses this episode to show both Scepticism's rhetorical power and Roman traditionalist resistance to Greek philosophy.

questions.prompt: What constructive doctrine did Carneades and Clitomachus develop despite denying the possibility of certain knowledge?
questions.answer: A doctrine of degrees of probability: although certainty is unattainable, some beliefs are more probable than others, and it is rational to act on the most probable available hypothesis. Russell notes most modern philosophers would agree with this view.
questions.explanation: This doctrine let the sceptical Academy oppose belief in divination, magic, and astrology on rational grounds.

flashcards.front: Who founded Cynicism, and from which earlier philosopher's circle did he come?
What does the word 'cynic' literally mean, and why was it applied to Diogenes?
flashcards.back: 'Canine' / 'dog-like' -- because Diogenes deliberately lived like a dog, rejecting shame and convention.

flashcards.front: What was Diogenes's famous reply when Alexander offered him any favour he wished?
flashcards.back: 'Only to stand out of my light.'

flashcards.front: What did popularized Cynic preacher Teles use the doctrine of indifference to justify?
flashcards.back: Minimizing a borrower's gratitude to a lender, and dismissing grief over the death of family as no reason to neglect one's own comfort.

flashcards.front: Who founded Scepticism as a formal school doctrine, and what military campaign had he been part of?
flashcards.back: Pyrrho, who accompanied Alexander's army as far as India.

flashcards.front: What is Russell's term for ancient Scepticism's actual character, as opposed to open-minded doubt?
flashcards.back: 'Dogmatic doubt' -- confidently asserting that nobody can ever know anything.

flashcards.front: What is Timon's regress argument against the possibility of proof?
flashcards.back: Deduction needs self-evident first principles; no such principles can be proven; so every argument is either circular or an endless unsupported chain, and nothing can be proved.

flashcards.front: Whom does Russell compare Timon to, regarding inference about unobserved entities like atoms?
Who turned Plato's Academy sceptical, and for roughly how long did this last?
flashcards.back: Arcesilaus; for about two hundred years.

flashcards.front: What happened in Carneades's two successive lectures at Rome in 156 B.C.?
flashcards.back: The first defended Plato/Aristotle's view of justice; the second demolished it, arguing that great states (including Rome) were built on successful injustice.

flashcards.front: Who was scandalized by Carneades's lectures and campaigned against Greek philosophical education at Rome?
What constructive epistemological doctrine did Carneades and Clitomachus develop?
flashcards.back: A doctrine of degrees of probability as a rational guide to action, despite the impossibility of certainty.

flashcards.front: Who revived pure (unmitigated) Scepticism after Clitomachus, rejecting the probability doctrine?
Who is the only ancient Sceptic philosopher whose works survive intact?
According to Sextus Empiricus's argument, what impious dilemma does affirming God's providence create?
flashcards.back: Either God controls everything (making Him the author of evil), or God controls only some or nothing (making Him grudging or impotent).

quiz.prompt: Who founded the Cynic school, tracing his own philosophical descent from a disciple of Socrates?
options: Pyrrho
Diogenes of Sinope
Zeno of Citium
Epicurus
quiz.explanation: Diogenes of Sinope, pupil of Antisthenes (himself a disciple of Socrates), founded and gave his name to the Cynic school's most famous practice.
quiz.related_concept: Cynic self-sufficiency through rejection of convention

quiz.prompt: What did Diogenes famously ask of Alexander the Great when offered any favour?
options: A large sum of gold
Safe passage to Athens
Only to stand out of his light
A position as royal tutor
quiz.explanation: This anecdote illustrates Diogenes's total indifference to worldly power and favour.
quiz.related_concept: Cynic self-sufficiency through rejection of convention

quiz.prompt: How does Russell distinguish philosophical Scepticism from ordinary scientific uncertainty?
options: Scepticism denies only sense-perception, while science denies logic
Scepticism dogmatically asserts that knowledge is impossible, while science holds tentative, revisable beliefs
Scepticism is a Roman doctrine, while science is purely Greek
There is no real difference in Russell's account
quiz.explanation: Russell calls Scepticism 'dogmatic doubt' precisely because it claims certainty about the impossibility of knowledge, unlike science's provisional caution.

quiz.prompt: What is the structure of Timon's argument that nothing can be proved?
options: All perception is illusory, so no factual claim can be trusted
Deduction requires self-evident first principles, none can be proven, so all argument is circular or an endless regress
Only mathematical claims can be proven, all others are opinion
The gods deliberately conceal truth from mortals
quiz.explanation: Timon's regress argument targets the structural requirement of Greek deductive logic for provable first premises.

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, Carneades's second Rome lecture in 156 B.C. was intended to sincerely establish that injustice is morally superior to justice.
options: True
False

Cato the Elder
Cicero
Marcus Aurelius

degrees of probability
majority opinion
astrological prediction
